content_html:
A stock split changes how many shares a company has and the price of each one, without changing what the company or your holding is worth. This calculator shows your share count, the adjusted price, your new cost basis per share, any cash paid for a fractional share, and how listed options on the stock are adjusted. It handles forward splits such as 2-for-1 and reverse splits such as 1-for-10.

How to use this calculator

  1. Shares you own: your current number of shares before the split.
  2. Share price before the split: the last price before the split takes effect.
  3. Split ratio: new shares for every old share. A 3-for-2 split is 3 new for 2 old; a 1-for-20 reverse split is 1 new for 20 old.
  4. Total cost basis (optional): what you paid for the shares in total. The split spreads that same amount across the new share count.
  5. Option contracts (optional): tick the box and enter your contracts and strike to see how they are adjusted.

How a split is calculated

Divide the new number in the ratio by the old one to get the split factor. Your shares are multiplied by the factor, and the price is divided by it:

shares after = shares × (new ÷ old) and price after = price ÷ (new ÷ old)

Because one goes up as the other goes down, the market value stays the same. Your total cost basis does not change either, so the basis per share is simply the total divided by the new share count. That new figure is what you compare with the sale price when you later sell.

Fractional shares and cash in lieu

Uneven ratios and reverse splits often leave a fraction of a share. Many companies pay that fraction out in cash instead of issuing it, at roughly the post-split price; some brokers credit the fraction instead. Part of your basis belongs to the fraction, and the cash payment is usually treated as a sale of that fraction, so it can create a small taxable gain or loss.

What happens to options

For listed US options, the Options Clearing Corporation adjusts contracts so the holder ends up in the same economic position. With a whole-number forward split such as 2-for-1 or 4-for-1, you usually receive more contracts at a lower strike, each still covering 100 shares. One contract with a $160 strike becomes two contracts at $80. With uneven ratios such as 3-for-2, and with reverse splits, the usual approach is to keep the number of contracts and the strike the same and change how many shares each contract delivers: 150 shares after a 3-for-2 split, or 10 shares after a 1-for-10 reverse split. These adjusted contracts can trade thinly. The exact terms appear in an information memo published for each corporate action, so check it before trading.

Things to keep in mind

  • A split does not make a stock cheaper in any real sense. Valuation measures such as the price-to-earnings ratio stay the same, because earnings per share are divided by the same factor.
  • Price targets, stop orders and alerts may need resetting. Brokers often cancel or adjust open orders around a split.
  • Historical prices on most charts are adjusted backward, so past prices may look lower than what you actually paid.

faq.question: Does a stock split change the value of my investment?
faq.answer: No. The split itself only divides the same value into more or fewer shares. Your holding is worth the same immediately before and after, apart from normal market movement and any small cash payment for a fractional share.

faq.question: Is a stock split a taxable event?
faq.answer: A standard split is generally not taxable in the United States because you receive nothing of value beyond more or fewer shares of the same company. Cash received for a fractional share is usually treated as a sale of that fraction. Your broker reports the details, and a tax professional can confirm your situation.

faq.question: What is the difference between a forward and a reverse split?
faq.answer: A forward split increases the number of shares and lowers the price, often after a big rise in the share price. A reverse split reduces the number of shares and raises the price, often so a low-priced stock can meet an exchange's minimum price rule.

faq.question: When does the new share count appear in my account?
faq.answer: The extra shares from a forward split usually appear on or shortly after the payable date, and the stock starts trading at the adjusted price on the ex-date. Your broker may show the old and new positions briefly while it processes the change.

faq.question: Why do I need my cost basis after a split?
faq.answer: When you sell, your gain or loss is the sale price minus your basis. After a split the total basis is unchanged but spread over a different number of shares, so the per-share figure changes. Brokers normally update it for you, but it is worth checking.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved.
